notes:
I found good coverage of the traditional reading and of the two places where interpreters really divide: God's instruction to Samuel in v. 2 and the "evil spirit" in vv. 14–23. I found much less on the other topics you asked about. Some things to know first:

- **Gaps:** I didn't find anything from the Lutheran or Orthodox sites, or anything on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. The only Catholic page I found (the Catholic Encyclopedia on newadvent.org) just retells the story. I had used up my searches and page reads before I could look further.
- **Missing verses:** The Enduring Word page cut off partway through v. 13, so its notes on vv. 14–23 are missing. I found nothing at all for v. 17.
- **Tradition labels:** Where I call a writer Methodist or Reformed, the label usually comes from the site's place on your list (Ligonier is Reformed, Enduring Word is under Pentecostal/charismatic). For Adam Clarke and Joseph Benson, the "Methodist" label is my own knowledge, not something the pages say.

---

**v. 1**
- Guzik: there is a time to mourn and a time to move on. God's work never dies with one man's failure. Jesse was the grandson of Ruth and Boaz. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- Guzik: God gave the people the kind of king they wanted (Saul), but stayed on the throne. The first king was anointed for the people; he was the "king from central casting", and now God would choose a king "for Me." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- Precept Austin: Samuel is still grieving from 15:35. Under Deuteronomy 17:15 the king was to be one "whom the LORD your God chooses." MacArthur adds that the new king, and finally the Messiah, comes from Judah and Bethlehem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary
- Matthew Henry: Saul was anointed from a small, brittle glass vial; David from a horn of oil, more plentiful and lasting. Henry links this to the "horn of salvation" in Luke 1:69. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/16-2.html
- NET note: the Hebrew literally reads "for I have seen among his sons for me a king." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16

**vv. 2–3 (debated: did God tell Samuel to deceive?)**
- Clarke (quoted by Guzik): no lie was told. Samuel really did offer the sacrifice and simply didn't reveal his main purpose. Doing so "would have produced evil and no good." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-samuel/1-samuel-16.cfm
- Coffman: "neither duplicity nor falsehood, but discretion and concealment, both of which are honorable." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/16-2.html
- Bible.org: God didn't tell the Bethlehem elders everything, but what He did say was absolutely true. Samuel did come to offer a sacrifice. https://bible.org/seriespage/designation-david-king-1-samuel-161-23
- Precept Austin admits the difficulty. It asks whether God encouraged deception here, and why God condemned Abraham for the same thing. Its answer is a clear distinction between actual deceit and withholding information that would cause great harm. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary
- A Bible Hub article cites Augustine's distinction between deliberate falsehood and careful silence, and says Samuel practices the latter. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_did_God_tell_Samuel_to_mislead_Saul.htm
- Guzik: Samuel's unusual fear may come from his excessive mourning. Note that God promised, "I will show you what to do." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/

**v. 4**
- Guzik: the elders' trembling makes sense given what Samuel had just done to Agag (15:33). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- NET text note: the Hebrew has "he said," but many manuscripts and ancient versions read "they said." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16
- Precept Austin: "O little town of Bethlehem": the Son of David would one day come from this same town. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary

**v. 5**
- Guzik: this was a fellowship-type offering. Part was burned and part was eaten at a ceremonial meal, unlike a sin offering, which was wholly burned. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- Henry: the family seems to have been devout. Samuel helped with their preparations and probably anointed David before the feast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/16-2.html

**v. 6**
- NET: "said to himself" is implied, because the mission was secret. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16
- Guzik: Samuel thought, in effect, "This man looks like a king." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/

**v. 7**
- Guzik: the verse is both a statement of fact and a call to godly thinking. Even Samuel judged by looks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- Matthew Poole: Samuel had already been fooled once by Saul's height (10:23–24) and shouldn't be fooled again. God would have chosen by the heart from the start if the people's sinful desires had not provoked him to give them a bad king. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-7.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: the Hebrew is literally "man looks at the eyes." The eyes stand for outward form. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-7.htm
- Gill: Jewish writers concluded that Eliab's heart was not right, perhaps full of wrath, pride or envy. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/amp/1-samuel/16-7.html
- Clarke: people should stick to judging outward appearance. Claiming to read hearts usurps the prerogative of God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/16-7.html
- NET text note (modern scholarship): the Hebrew is shortened ("for not that which the man sees"). NET follows the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), saying the Hebrew lost words through a copying slip, and cites McCarter. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16

**vv. 8–10**
- Guzik: the older sons weren't bad men, but they were not God's choice. Israel already had a king "after the flesh." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- NET note on "seven sons": 1 Samuel 17:12 gives Jesse eight sons, but 1 Chronicles 2:13–15 lists only seven including David. 1 Chronicles 27:18 names another son, Elihu. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16

**v. 11**
- Guzik: this shows how little David was regarded. He isn't named, wasn't invited, and is called only at Samuel's insistence. Shepherding was servant's work, but it was training time, not waiting time (Psalm 78:70–72). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- NET translates the last clause as "we cannot turn our attention to other things until he comes." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16

**v. 12**
- Guzik: "ruddy" probably means a fair complexion, and bright eyes suggest vitality. David was attractive but didn't look like a "born king" the way Saul did. Josephus says he was about 10; others guess about 15. What made him "the one" was being a man after God's heart (13:14). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- Precept Austin notes the Greek Old Testament reads, "anoint David, for he is good." https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary

**v. 13**
- Guzik: only God and Samuel probably understood what this anointing meant. It is also the first time the name "David" appears in 1 Samuel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- MacArthur (via Precept Austin): this was the first of three anointings. The other two (2 Samuel 2:4; 5:3) made him king publicly over Judah and then all Israel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary
- Precept Austin: the Spirit was supernatural empowerment for service; the oil on his head symbolized the Spirit in his heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary
- Ligonier (Reformed): in David the Spirit came both to empower and to save. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/spiritual-transformations
- Kingcomments: David is anointed among his brothers, Saul alone. This mirrors Jesus taking his place among the faithful remnant at his baptism. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-samuel-16.html
- Constable: Samuel's anointing of David was the climax and capstone of his career. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-samuel/16-2.html

**v. 14 (the main point of difference)**

*What did Saul lose?*
- Benson and Poole: God took away the gifts that fitted Saul to be king, such as prudence and courage. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- Clarke: "what God fills not, the devil will." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/1-samuel/16-14.html
- Ligonier (Reformed): the Spirit came on Saul as on the judges. His conduct shows there was no work of regeneration in him. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/spiritual-transformations
- Kingcomments: this does not mean Saul was a believer and then stopped being one. He was never a believer, and the verse is not about the Spirit living within him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/1-samuel-16.html
- Bible.org: the Spirit's presence or absence in the Old Testament says nothing about salvation. It speaks only of power for service. https://bible.org/question/why-did-spirit-god-make-saul-lay-naked-samuel
- GotQuestions: in the Old Testament the Spirit "came upon" people for a time. Since the resurrection his indwelling is permanent, and we cannot lose the Holy Spirit. https://www.gotquestions.org/lose-the-Holy-Spirit.html
- F.B. Meyer is gentler: it does not necessarily mean that all the religious life of Saul had become extinct, only that his power for kingship was withdrawn. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/meyer/an_evil_spirit_from_the_lord.htm

*What was the "evil spirit"?*
- Demonic reading: Keil & Delitzsch call it a higher evil power, which took possession of him. Poole says take "evil spirit" in its plain sense; God let the devil trouble Saul. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- Bible.org: it was a demonic, satanic instrument. https://bible.org/question/why-did-spirit-god-make-saul-lay-naked-samuel
- Psychological reading: the Commentary Critical and Explanatory traces it to Saul's own gloomy reflections, which made him subject to fits of morbid melancholy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- Chandler (quoted in Bible Hub sermons) calls it a spirit of melancholy, jealousy and envy. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- Mixed reading: the Treasury of Scripture Knowledge says his malady appears to have been of a mixed kind, natural and diabolical. https://www.studylight.org/bible/spa/bla/1-samuel/16-14.html

*In what sense was it "from the LORD"?*
- Benson: "by God's permission, who delivered him up to be buffeted by Satan." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- GotQuestions: God allowed it as judgment for Saul's two acts of disobedience. https://www.gotquestions.org/evil-spirit-Saul.html
- Meyer: Hebrew often says God does what he permits. https://biblehub.com/sermons/auth/meyer/an_evil_spirit_from_the_lord.htm
- Ligonier: God gave the spirit greater-than-usual liberty to torment Saul. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/spiritual-transformations
- The Gospel Coalition (McDonald): God sent the evil spirit to judge Saul's persistent disobedience. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/god-made-god-tempt-saul-evil-spirit/
- Leckie (Bible Hub sermons) adds that the torment was meant to push Saul to turn and cry to God for help. https://biblehub.com/sermons/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- NET note (modern scholarship): it can be rendered "injurious spirit" and need not refer to an evil, demonic spirit. "Evil" may describe its effect on Saul ("a mischief-making spirit"). https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16

**vv. 15–16**
- Cambridge Bible: it is called "an evil spirit of God" because it was God's messenger of judgment, but never "the Spirit of the LORD." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch make the same point. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm

**v. 18**
- NET: "eloquent" is literally "discerning of word," and "handsome" is "a man of form." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16
- Bible.org: others praised David as a "brave warrior," which contrasts with Eliab's scorn for him in chapter 17. https://bible.org/seriespage/18-david-becomes-israel-s-king-1-samuel-16-2-samuel-10

**v. 19**
- Guzik: David simply went back to the sheep after being anointed. Either he didn't yet understand, or he knew it was God's job to put him on the throne. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-16/
- Epp and Precept Austin: this reflects a humble, faithful heart. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary

**vv. 20–22**
- Precept Austin calls it a great irony: the newly anointed king-to-be ministers to the rejected king. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-16-commentary
- NET: "Saul admired him" is literally "he loved him." "Let David remain" is literally "let David stand before me." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=1Sa&chapter=16

**v. 23**
- Cambridge: the cause was "supernatural," the cure "natural." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- Matthew Henry warns that music can also be misused to draw the heart from God, and that is driving away the good Spirit, not the evil spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_samuel/16-14.htm
- GotQuestions: the evil spirit that troubled Saul was only temporary. https://www.gotquestions.org/evil-spirit-Saul.html
- Bible Hub study notes see David's soothing music as foreshadowing Christ, the Shepherd-King who brings peace. https://biblehub.com/study/1_samuel/16-14.htm

**Catholic (whole chapter)**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia simply retells the story. Samuel was sent to anoint the shepherd lad in place of Saul, whom God had rejected for disobedience. I found no Catholic comment on the debated verses. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/04642b.htm
